title: “LET THE DEAD BURY THEIR OWN DEAD” — WHY WOULD JESUS SAY SOMETHING THAT SOUNDS SO HARSH?
paragraphs:
“LET THE DEAD BURY THEIR OWN DEAD” — WHY WOULD JESUS SAY SOMETHING THAT SOUNDS SO HARSH?
One of Jesus’ most disturbing sentences may actually be one of His most urgent invitations to life—and the word hidden inside the disciple’s response may expose the excuse standing between you and Christ.
There are words of Jesus we love putting on walls.
“Come to me.”
“Do not be afraid.”
“Peace be with you.”
And then there are words like these.
“Let the dead bury their own dead.”
You read that sentence and something inside you almost recoils.
Jesus…
Really?
A man wants to bury his father, and that is Your answer?
Where is the compassion?
Where is the tenderness?
Where is the Jesus who wept at Lazarus’ tomb?

Maybe you have buried someone you loved. Maybe you have stood beside a coffin wishing you could hear one more laugh, receive one more embrace, say one more sentence you assumed you would have time to say.
If so, these words can sound especially brutal.
But before we accuse Jesus of lacking compassion, we need to slow down.
Because the Jesus who spoke these words is also the Jesus who wept when Lazarus died.
The Jesus who noticed a grieving widow walking behind the body of her only son.
The Jesus who, while hanging from a cross and struggling for breath, still made provision for His mother.
So whatever Luke 9:60 means, it cannot honestly mean that Jesus considers grief meaningless or that honoring family is sinful.
Something deeper is happening.
And when you see it, this strange sentence stops looking like an attack on grieving people.
It becomes a terrifyingly personal question:
What have you placed between the words “Lord” and “follow”?
Luke records the encounter with almost uncomfortable simplicity.
Jesus says to a man:
“Follow me.”
The man answers:
“Lord, first let me go and bury my father.”
Then comes the sentence that has disturbed readers for centuries:
“Let the dead bury their own dead, but you go and proclaim the kingdom of God.”
Matthew preserves the same piercing exchange and places the emphasis directly on Jesus’ call:
“Follow me, and let the dead bury their own dead.”
Matthew 8:22.
But there is something in the conversation that is easy to miss.
The New Testament was written here in Greek, and Luke’s Greek makes the collision startling.
Jesus’ invitation is:
Ἀκολούθει μοι — Akolouthei moi.
“Follow Me.”
But the man’s response contains a tiny word carrying enormous weight:
πρῶτον — prōton.
“First.”
Lord…
first.
That may be where this entire story opens.
The problem is not merely that the man wants to bury his father.
The problem exposed by the narrative is the question of priority.
Jesus says, “Follow Me.”
The man effectively answers, “Yes, Lord…but first.”
And suddenly this ancient conversation becomes painfully modern.
“Lord, I’ll follow You…but first let me get my life together.”
“Jesus, I’ll surrender…but first let me enjoy this relationship.”
“I’ll forgive…but first they need to apologize.”
“I’ll repent…but first let me have a little more time.”
“I’ll serve You…but first let me become financially secure.”
“I’ll tell people about You…but first let me stop being afraid of what they think.”
“I’ll come back to church…but first I need to fix myself.”
“I’ll open my Bible again…but first life needs to calm down.”
“I’ll follow You, Lord…
but first.”
And perhaps some of the most dangerous words a human being can say to Jesus are not, “I hate You.”
They are:
“Not yet.”
Because “not yet” feels nothing like rebellion.
It feels reasonable.
Responsible.
Temporary.
Even respectable.
That is what makes it dangerous.
We need to be careful, however, not to manufacture historical certainty Scripture itself does not give us.
Was the man’s father already dead?
Was the funeral happening immediately?
Was “bury my father” a way of asking to remain home until his father eventually died?
Was Jesus’ statement connected with burial practices in which remains could later be gathered and reinterred?

Interpreters have proposed several possibilities. Ancient Jewish burial customs can illuminate the passage, and some commentators argue that the request may involve obligations extending beyond an immediate funeral. But the text itself does not give us enough information to declare every historical detail with certainty.
And perhaps we should not become so fascinated with reconstructing the man’s family circumstances that we miss what Luke actually tells us.
Jesus gives the meaning of the moment through the contrast:
The dead may bury their dead.
“But you…”
You have been called somewhere else.
You have been summoned to announce the Kingdom of God.
That “but you” changes everything.
The Greek of Luke 9:60 reads:
Ἄφες τοὺς νεκροὺς θάψαι τοὺς ἑαυτῶν νεκρούς· σὺ δὲ ἀπελθὼν διάγγελλε τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ.
In straightforward English:
“Leave the dead to bury their own dead; but you, having gone, proclaim the kingdom of God.”
The shock is deliberate.
Jesus speaks of “dead” people burying “dead” people.
Obviously a physically dead person cannot conduct a funeral.

That is precisely why interpreters have long understood the first use of “dead” as referring in some sense to those outside the life and calling of the Kingdom, while the second refers to the physically deceased. Luke’s command immediately turns the disciple toward proclamation of God’s Kingdom.
Jesus is forcing a distinction between two kinds of existence.
There is breathing.
And there is life.
There is existing.
And there is following Christ.
There is maintaining everything expected of you.
And there is hearing the King call your name.
This is not Jesus saying funerals do not matter.
This is Jesus saying He matters ultimately.
That difference is enormous.
The same Lord who commands people to honor father and mother will not allow even something honorable to become greater than obedience to Him.
Because good things can become dangerous things when they become first things.
Family is good.
Work is good.
Responsibility is good.
Security is good.
Reputation can be good.
Planning can be wise.
But none of them can occupy the throne.
Only Christ belongs there.
And this is where the passage stops being an ancient theological puzzle and begins walking through your front door.
Because your “father’s burial” may not look anything like this man’s.
Yours might be the relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
The secret habit you keep promising to surrender eventually.
The resentment you have rehearsed for so long that anger now feels like part of your identity.
The career that has slowly become your god.
The approval of people whose opinions have become louder than Scripture.
The pornography nobody knows about.
The compromise you have renamed “struggling” because calling it sin would require repentance.
The church wound you now use as permission to stay far from Jesus.
The shame that whispers you need to clean yourself before you can come home.
The comfortable Christianity where Jesus can inspire you, encourage you, bless you, protect you and forgive you…
as long as He never interrupts your plans.
Then Christ walks directly into all of it.
And says:
Follow Me.
Not when you become impressive.
Not when your history becomes less embarrassing.
Not when temptation disappears.
Not when everybody understands.
Not after you have repaired yourself.
Follow Me.
And perhaps you whisper:
“Lord…”
That sounds promising.
“…first…”
And heaven suddenly touches the nerve.
Because Jesus is not applying for second place in your life.
He is Lord.
There is something else here we desperately need to understand.
Jesus’ severity is not the opposite of His love.
Sometimes it is an expression of it.
A doctor who discovers something deadly inside you does not love you by pretending everything is fine.
A firefighter does not whisper politely while your bedroom fills with smoke.
And Christ does not flatter us while we sleep spiritually beside things that are killing us.
Grace is tender.
But grace is not tame.
Jesus receives sinners, but He does not tell us our chains are jewelry.
He forgives the guilty, but He does not rename darkness light.
He welcomes the broken, but He loves them too much to leave them worshiping what broke them.
That is why Christianity cannot be reduced to “Jesus makes me feel better.”
Jesus did not merely come to improve your mood.
He came to save sinners.
He came to reconcile rebels to God.
He came to forgive.
To redeem.
To resurrect.
To make dead hearts alive.
And eventually His road leads to another shocking scene.
Not a funeral.
A cross.
There, the One who told a man to leave the dead and proclaim the Kingdom would Himself be numbered among the dead.
Nails through His hands.
Blood running down wood.
Mockery around Him.
Darkness overhead.
His disciples scattered.
His body placed inside a borrowed tomb.
If Luke 9 were the only picture we possessed of Jesus, someone might accuse Him of being indifferent toward death.
But Calvary destroys that accusation.
Jesus does not stand safely outside human death and shout instructions at us.
He enters it.
He bears sin.
He tastes death.
He is buried.
And on the third day, the tomb loses.
That is the Gospel.
Not that good people learn how to become slightly better people.
Not that religious people earn enough points for heaven.
Not that broken people pretend they were never broken.
The Gospel announces that sinners who cannot save themselves can be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
The crucified Christ rises.
Grace walks out of the grave.
And suddenly “let the dead bury their own dead” sounds different.
Because the Man saying it is walking toward the place where He will conquer death.
He is calling this disciple away from death toward the announcement of a Kingdom where death will not have the final word.
That is why following Jesus cannot permanently remain somewhere near the bottom of your schedule.
If Christ really rose from the dead, Christianity cannot merely be your inspirational accessory.
If Christ really bore our sins, repentance cannot be treated as an optional religious hobby.
If Christ really is Lord, “later” cannot safely become the permanent answer to His call.
And maybe that is why you are still reading.
Maybe something inside you has been uncomfortable for several paragraphs.
Not because you hate Jesus.
Because you know exactly what your “first” is.
You already thought of it.
That name.
That habit.
That wound.
That secret.
That excuse.
That compromise.
That room inside your heart where you keep telling Christ:
“Everything is Yours…
except this.”
Listen carefully.
Jesus is not calling you to earn His grace.
You cannot.
He is not telling you to become worthy enough to approach Him.
You cannot do that either.
The scandal of grace is that Christ came for sinners.
Real ones.
Messy ones.
Ashamed ones.
People with histories.
People with addictions.
People who failed after promising God they never would again.
People who knew better and still chose wrong.
People who have sat in church while hiding things that would shock everyone sitting beside them.
People like us.
Repentance does not mean purchasing forgiveness with enough tears.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior who alone can save.
Grace is not God pretending your sin never mattered.
Look at the cross.
It mattered enough for Christ to bleed.
And the cross is not God declaring that you are beyond redemption.
Look at the empty tomb.
Jesus rewrites endings.
That is why our heartbeat at Gospel Warrior remains:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Peter denied Him.
Jesus restored him.
Thomas doubted.
Jesus met him.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Christ transformed him into a preacher of the faith he once tried to destroy.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left to repair his reputation, build a ministry, repay society or impress religious people.
He had a dying body, a guilty history and faith placed in a crucified King.
Grace met him there.
Your scandal does not have to write your final chapter either.
But grace is not permission to keep running.
Grace calls you home.
So maybe today the prayer is not complicated.
“Jesus, no more ‘but first.’”
No more negotiating.
No more pretending.
No more hiding.
No more trying to make peace with the thing Christ is calling you to surrender.
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes bringing a struggle into the light is the first honest moment we have allowed ourselves in a very long time.
Let believers who see your words pray with you.
Your testimony may become the reason somebody else realizes they are not beyond the reach of grace.
Someone reading those three words may need them tonight.
Not because sharing a Facebook post earns favor with God. It does not.
It does not.

But if this message is faithful to Scripture and you believe someone in your circle needs to hear it, sharing it is one practical way you can help place biblical truth in front of another human being.
Send it privately to the person whose faith has gone quiet.
Send it to the believer carrying secret shame.
Send it to the person who believes Jesus could forgive everyone except them.
Even send it to the skeptical friend who thinks Christianity is only condemnation and rules.
Let them encounter the scandal of a Savior who tells sinners the truth and then goes to the cross to save them.
Because there may come a night when you need to read it again.
Your support helps Gospel-centered teaching keep reaching people.
But before you leave this article, go back to that road in Luke one last time.
Imagine the dust.
Imagine Jesus standing there.
Imagine the disciple facing Him.
No stage.
No microphone.
No audience.
Just a man…
and Christ.
“Follow Me.”
“Lord, first…”
We never hear the rest of this man’s story.
Luke does not tell us whether he followed.
Maybe that silence is intentional.
Because eventually the question stops being about him.
It becomes about us.
Jesus has already walked toward Jerusalem.
Already carried the cross.
Already entered death.
Already risen.
Already opened the way for sinners to be reconciled to God.
And now, across centuries, through the pages of Scripture, His call still reaches people buried beneath shame, distraction, religion, ambition, grief, compromise and delay.
Follow Me.
Maybe you have spent years explaining why today cannot be the day.
Maybe everyone around you thinks you are spiritually fine.
Maybe nobody knows what happens when the screen goes dark and you are alone with your thoughts.
Maybe you have learned Christian vocabulary while slowly drifting from Christ Himself.
Maybe you have been standing beside your excuse for so long that you started calling it wisdom.
But Jesus is still calling.
Not toward condemnation for everyone who comes to Him in faith.
Toward life.
Toward repentance.
Toward forgiveness.
Toward grace.
Toward Himself.
So when Christ says, “Follow Me,” may our answer finally lose two devastating words.
Not:
“Lord, but first…”
Just:
“Lord.”
And perhaps the sentence that sounded cruel at the beginning was actually the sound of Life Himself calling a human being out of the kingdom of death.
And comment honestly before you leave.
What is your “but first”?
You do not need to tell the whole story.
Maybe all you can write is:
Sometimes surrender begins when the sentence we have spent years avoiding finally leaves our heart.
And remember this when your past starts shouting louder than the cross:
The grave may describe where you have been—but when Jesus calls your name, it does not get to decide where your story ends.
